data.title: Spišské Tomášovce – a hillfort of the Principality of Nitra in Spiš
data.excerpt: On a limestone crag above the confluence of the Hornád and the Tomášovský Brook stood a major hillfort of the Principality of Nitra, with a carefully built, stone-faced chambered timber-and-earth rampart and a pincer-shaped main gate. Peter Šalkovský, who published partial results of his detailed excavation in 2006, reconstructed the height and appearance of its defences; this article draws above all on his work.
data.metaTitle: Spišské Tomášovce – hillfort of the Principality of Nitra
data.metaDescription: A major hillfort of the Principality of Nitra on the boundary of the Slovak Paradise and the Hornád Basin, excavated and reconstructed by Peter Šalkovský.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Left bank of the Hornád at its confluence with the Tomášovský Brook, on the boundary of the Slovak Paradise and the Hornád Basin; acropolis on a limestone crag at 540–567 m a.s.l.

keyFacts.label: Area
keyFacts.value: The bailey terrace about 3 ha (a roughly trapezoidal enclosure), together with the acropolis 5–6 ha; ramparts with a total length of around 600 m

keyFacts.label: Rampart construction
keyFacts.value: A front drystone wall of quarried stone with chambered (in places grillage) timber-and-earth bracing; most massive by the north-eastern gate (3.9–4 m in total)

keyFacts.label: North-western corner
keyFacts.value: A “bastion-like” structure with three fan-shaped timber chambers, strengthened by a stone cross-wall at least 2.5 m wide

keyFacts.label: Main gate
keyFacts.value: Pincer-shaped type, western wing 7.8 m long; entrance 2.8 m wide, narrowing inwards to 2 m

keyFacts.label: Estimated height of the defences
keyFacts.value: Average rampart 1.6–2.1 m, most massive 2.1–2.6 m; with the palisade breastwork up to 3.6–4.1 m in total in the northern rampart

keyFacts.label: Regional context
keyFacts.value: One of 14 published Slovak hillforts with the same fortification technique (together with Pobedim, Bojná, Nitra, Devín and others)

children.text: A major hillfort of the Principality of Nitra in eastern Slovakia has been studied in detail in recent times above all by Peter Šalkovský, who published partial results of his excavations in 2006. The following article draws chiefly on the results of his research.

The site of Hradisko I lies on the boundary between the Slovak Paradise (Slovenský raj) and the Hornád Basin and between the cadastral areas of the villages of Spišské Tomášovce and Smižany (Spišská Nová Ves District), on the left bank of the Hornád at its confluence with the Tomášovský Brook. Although the name Hradisko I was originally applied only to the limestone crag (540–567 m above sea level), whose plateau is fortified and where the acropolis was presumed to lie, today we use it for the whole site, that is, also for the immediate surroundings, which are divided into three sites. The hillfort consisted of an “acropolis” set on the dominant crag and of a “bailey, or baileys”, on the relatively flat western and north-eastern foreground.

The technique, material and quality of the fortification of the “acropolis” of Hradisko I (site 1) and of the western “bailey” (site 3, or Pod hradiskom) are similar, but we do not know the quality of the internal buildings and of the use of the “acropolis”. It is certain that both sites were part of a single fortified whole in the period in question. The fortified enclosure of the “western bailey” must, from the military and of course also from the functional point of view, have formed a single whole with the elevated “acropolis” lacking fortification and military control (fortifying the terrace alone would make practically no sense). In some publications the site is also inaccurately called the Čingov hillfort.

The relatively flat terrace of the Tomášovský Brook was divided into two parts. The dominant part was fortified with ramparts on three sides — north, west and south — and thus formed a roughly trapezoidal enclosure with an area of about 3 ha at an elevation of 507–527 m. On the fourth — eastern — side (c. 297 m long) the ramparts joined almost perpendicularly to the steeply rising rocky slope of the hillfort, whose summit plateau lies at an elevation of 560–567 m. In the investigation of the main “bailey” enclosure the northern rampart was almost completely uncovered, along with 90 m of the western rampart.

The construction of the rampart and its dimensions were not uniform. The front, so-called drystone wall of quarried stone was preserved in situ in three almost continuous stretches (10–70 cm high, together c. 135 m long) in the northern and western ramparts. This was mostly coursed masonry, laid fairly carefully, without any discernible bonding material. A timber chambered construction was attested above all in a large part of the northern rampart in the form of strips of subsoil burnt to brick hardness — a kind of thermal “imprint” of the burnt chambers. The overall width of the fortification was not uniform. It was most massive in the eastern part of the northern rampart — by the north-eastern gate, where the front facing reached as much as 1.35–1.4 m and the timber-and-earth body 2.50–2.65 m (thus 3.9–4 m in total). The remainder of the northern rampart was slightly more slender. The ends of the transverse beams were at one end partly connected with the front wall, while at the other end they projected beyond the line of the inner timber wall of the chambers.

children.text: Specially reinforced construction was used at the strategically and structurally most sensitive points — the north-western corner, the gate in the north-eastern corner, and the gate and also the culvert in the western part of the northern rampart. At the north-western corner the space between two long chambers was strengthened by a massive stone cross-wall at least 2.5 m wide running across the whole width of the rampart. Similar cross-walls, 80–100 cm wide, reinforced from both sides the “bastion-like” structure of the corner, braced inside by three trapezoidal, fan-shaped timber chambers with transverse beams sunk deep into the front facing, which was strengthened to c. 100 cm. Comparable reinforcing cross-walls were also found, for example, in the north-western stretch of the acropolis fortification at Mikulčice.

The absence of traces of small chambers, or rather the long chambers to the east and south of the “corner bastion”, has been interpreted as dwellings built into the body of the rampart. This is supported by traces of floors and finds of small objects, as well as by the reinforcement of the rampart with cross-walls not only directly in the corner but also on the western side of the third such feature. The western wing of the main gate, 7.8 m long, faced with the same technique as the whole rampart, that is of broken conglomerate and sandstone, was preserved to a height of 60 cm. It projected almost 5 m inwards into the enclosure and reached a thickness of over 2 m at the corner. On the inside it ended in a large post hole 27 cm in diameter (probably part of the gate system). The entrance was about 2.8 m wide at the front, narrowing slightly obliquely inwards to c. 2 m. Such a gate belongs to the pincer-shaped type. The course of the approach road may be assumed to have run straight from the north along the slope of the acropolis. The ditch did not continue as far as the gate (probably for structural reasons). It ended 3 m to the west, and in the space between, post holes were found which suggest the existence of a kind of short outlying palisade screen.

In the north-western foreground of the fortification it is realistic to assume at the least waterlogged ground flooded by the brook, perhaps even a partly artificial body of water — a small reservoir created by means of a dam somewhat lower down the Tomášovský Brook. The water surface probably contributed to increasing the safety of the bailey. At the eastern edge of the terrace, at the point where it joins the acropolis, a semicircular rampart about 25 m in diameter and 2–2.2 m wide, bonded with the subsoil, was investigated. In front of the northern rampart, sections revealed a ditch 1.8–2 m deep and 7.5–8 m wide over a length of almost 100 m. It was absent in front of the entrance in the north-eastern corner.

The overall ground plan of the settlement complex and the placing of the ramparts were determined by the terrain relief of the site. In the east the northern rampart is anchored at the point where the acropolis begins to rise more markedly and to stand out above the surrounding terrain. Westwards this rampart was laid out in an almost straight line, not however along the contours but across them, that is, straight towards the point where the height drop of the terrace above the lower-lying Tomášovský Brook begins, which continues in still more massive form along the whole of the western and southern ramparts. The southern rampart is anchored to the acropolis at the point where its sides begin to be formed by the rocky crags of the Hornád gorge. The shorter outlying northern rampart blocked communication perpendicularly across the most accessible terrain from the Hornád Basin and created a kind of defensive foreground here.

children.text: The type of rampart of the main enclosure, with an outer stone wall and an inner timber — in places also stone — wall, with a core of varied timber-and-earth, chiefly chambered construction, occurring in several variations, represents the principal fortification technique of Slavic Middle Danubian (Great Moravian) defensive architecture in the 9th century. From the territory of Slovakia, 14 such sites have been published — Pobedim, Mužla, Bratislava-Devínska Nová Ves (Na pieskoch and Nad lomom), Bratislava-Hrad, Jur pri Bratislave, Tlmače, Hronský Beňadik (with a front stone wall and an inner timber wall), Nitra-Hrad (ramparts I and II), Nitra-Martinský vrch, Bojná, Majcichov, Detva. In Moravia and Bohemia about 10 such sites have been identified (e.g. Mikulčice, Břeclav-Pohansko, Sudomérice, Uherské Hradište, Nejdek, Tašovice), and at others such a fortification technique may be assumed. Evidence of similar defences is also known from the area between the Elbe and the Saale in the Lusatian Sorbian territories, where it is generally connected with East Frankish influence on the local Slavic defensive architecture. The facings of the Tomášovce fortification were built fairly carefully, chiefly of flat-broken stone. The shape of the burnt subsoil indicates a chambered reinforcement of the rampart body, probably formed by classic log chambers with a drystone facing at the front and, at least in places, a rear wall strengthened with vertical posts or with a more slender, lower stone facing. Compared with grillage or tie-beam framing, chambered framing represents a more perfect way of ensuring the stability of the rampart, since it eliminated the negative action of horizontal forces. We know of no analogies to the long chambers in the body of the Tomášovce rampart.

At Spišské Tomášovce the main technology — log chambers — was supplemented at the base by a grillage of laid timbers, and the inner wall of the rampart was strengthened with vertical beams. The log chambers of the rampart here were probably not built consistently everywhere; in places more material-saving and less laborious techniques of reinforcing the rampart were chosen, using untrimmed and unbranched trunks, and even incorporating into its body the lower parts of trees growing in the line of the rampart.

Overall we assume a height of the defences of 1.6–2.1 m for the average rampart and 2.1–2.6 m for the most massive stone-faced earthen body. This was evidently raised still further by a breastwork formed of a palisade wall (the existence of such walls is generally not doubted), whose height above the body of the rampart was functionally determined by the height of the defenders’ torsos and which was anchored at approximately the same depth in the reinforcement of the rampart behind the front facing. It is assumed that in the final phase the rampart was defended chiefly with hand-held cutting and thrusting weapons (spear, axe, sword), so the palisade could not be higher than the defenders’ outstretched arms (given an average height of 1.65 m for the Great Moravian male population), which could be around 1.35 m. If a low timber wall-walk is assumed, it could evidently have been somewhat more, at least around 1.5 m. The total height of the Tomášovce fortification including the palisade breastwork could thus have been c. 2.6–3.6 m above the western slope and around 3.6 to 4.1 m in the northern rampart. There are no indications of any treatment of the crown of the rampart, which it was certainly necessary to protect against being soaked by rain. In principle this could most effectively have been prevented by simple roofing, but also by covering with planks or with turf, that is, by grassing it over. Shallower ditches probably served to protect the foundations against saturation by surface water. Such a ditch was found along the northern rampart, discharging outside the fortified area through a culvert or opening beneath the rampart.

It is evident that the greatest effort and the greatest quantity of material were invested in the northern rampart, which cut across the almost level approach terrain from the relatively flat Hornád Basin and in which both gates were situated. This is attested by the strengthening of the whole rampart, but especially of its parts by the gate, by the digging of a ditch up to 2 m deep and 7–8 m wide, and by the probable use of the waters of the Tomášovský Brook to flood the surroundings of the north-western spur of the fortified enclosure, as well as by the “bastion-like” or tower-like design of the north-western corner, which made it possible to protect the ramparts better by archery. We know such reinforcing elements from later medieval fortifications, where bastions projected from the line of the main wall, which made it possible to shoot along the space at the foot of the defences and to cross-shoot the foreground. Unlike a bastion, a tower reached a greater height than the adjoining stretches of wall with which it was connected by walkways, which also gave the defenders an advantage. A similar tower-like platform may also be assumed above both gates, especially above the massive structure of the gate in the north-eastern corner of the defences.

Compared with ramparts with a timber front wall, fortifications with a stone facing were more resistant to fire and to being breached. Their structural properties, however, did not allow shell-construction walls with drystone walling to be built much higher than 4 m, which did not constitute an insurmountable obstacle. For reasons of defence, therefore, not only the height of the rampart was important but also the width of the wall-walk, which, if the first attackers broke through onto the crown of the wall, made it possible to concentrate further defenders at the threatened spot. In practice, however, this was limited by the consumption of building materials. The top of the rampart naturally always had to be narrower than the base. Ramparts with sloping sides did theoretically allow building to an unlimited height, but only with a simultaneous widening of the rampart. The higher the rampart was to be, the wider it had to be, and thus the more building material was needed for its construction. The real quantity of timber and stone which the given community was able to gather and work was probably decisive in designing its parameters. A high proportion of timber probably prevented mechanical disruption sufficiently, but such ramparts were more at risk from fire, by which they were in the end also put out of action. Whether this happened in the course of a siege, or only as part of the intentional devastation of an opponent’s infrastructure after the hillfort had been taken, we learn only rarely in individual cases.
On the dating and significance of the fortification

The starting arguments for dating the rampart were provided by several find contexts, above all features close to the rampart and covered by its destruction debris. The period in which the rampart existed is probably represented by features containing archaic pottery, a spur with hooks, a Late Avar bronze tongue-shaped strap end with S-shaped plant ornament, and a bronze earring, with a possible dating from the end of the 8th to the middle of the 9th century.

The period after the demise of the rampart is indicated by a spur with triangular … coming from the upper layer above the destruction of the rampart. The analogies (Břeclav-Pohansko, Bratislava, Devín) are dated to the second half of the 9th century or to the classic Great Moravian horizon. By then probably only an open settlement existed here, whose duration we provisionally date in broad terms to the second half of the 9th century and the 10th century. Massive traces of burning on the rampart testify to its destruction by fire. Only as working hypotheses can we describe the suggestions linking its demise with the process of state formation sometime in the first half of the 9th century and with the incorporation of the territory of Spiš into the Moravian state. These suggestions and this chronology are supported by finds of isolated children’s graves at the site behind the Flóra hotel, which contained silver grape-cluster earrings with a decorated lower arc, of Byzantine-Oriental character, datable to the end of the 9th century and surviving into the first half of the 10th century. It is probably with this period, that is, with the classic Great Moravian and post-Great Moravian period, that the emergence and functioning of the second hillfort (Hradisko II) corresponds, situated about 800 m to the south-west on the right bank of the Hornád, on a promontory (530–540 m above sea level) of the Čingov hill, known from field surveys and smaller test-trenching operations. The semicircular rampart-like feature inside the enclosure was probably originally built in the Roman period and, during the existence of the Slavic hillfort, was again reconstructed and used within the existing defensive system of the site. The kind of fortification used and the types of residential architecture on the terrace of the Tomášovský Brook indicate its intensive use both for habitation and for economic life. By the character and length of its ramparts and by its area, this enclosure ranks among the medium-sized hillforts. The area of the terrace, with an extent of approximately 3.3 ha, was fortified with ramparts of a total length of around 600 m (520 + 80 m). In the spectrum of hillforts from the territory of Slovakia it ranks by area ahead of the hillforts of Jur pri Bratislave, Starý Tekov, Tlmače, Kozmálovce, Hronský Beňadik and Zemplín. Together with the acropolis, which for reasons of defence necessarily had to be part of a single fortified whole, this site reached around 5–6 ha, which is roughly comparable with the hillforts at Jaseňové, Devín and at Bratislava Castle. The Tomášovce hillfort, however, did not attain the dimensions, nor probably the economic and military importance, of the hillforts at Pobedim, Majcichov, Bojná and Nitra, nor of the central Moravian hillforts.

The fortification and material culture of the hillfort reflect not only the regional particularities of the local Slavic occupation in the period from the 8th to the 10th century, but also its interactions both with the Principality of Nitra and Great Moravia to the south-west and with the Polish tribes of the Vistula region to the north.
Summary:
Hillfort I – Spišské Tomášovce

A second wave of Slavic colonisation of the Spiš region took place during the 7th and 8th centuries. Settlement was most intense at Čingov in the Slovak Paradise (Slovenský raj), where a large fortification of the Principality of Nitra was built in what is now eastern Slovakia. By around the middle of the 8th century the hillfort's fortifications had been completed, and construction had begun on the defensive works of the extramural settlement (the outer bailey). Such a precisely built Slavic hillfort dating from the pre–Great Moravian period was previously unknown in Slovakia. In some publications the site is inaccurately referred to as the Čingov hillfort.

The fortified area, covering roughly 12 hectares, consists of the hillfort proper (400 × 300 m) and its outer bailey (podhradisko). Hillfort I (Hradisko I), located at coordinates N 48°56.7839′, E 20°29.3900′, lies on the boundary between the Slovak Paradise and the Hornád Basin, within the cadastral areas of the villages of Spišské Tomášovce and Smižany (Spišská Nová Ves District), on the left bank of the Hornád River at its confluence with the Tomášovský Brook.

Although the name Hradisko I originally referred only to the limestone cliff (540–567 m above sea level) — whose plateau is fortified and is presumed to have held the acropolis — today the name is applied to the entire site, including the immediate surroundings, which are divided into three sections. The fortification consisted of the "acropolis," situated on the dominant rocky outcrop, and the "outer bailey" (the settlement below the hillfort), located on the relatively flat foreground to the west and northeast.

The type of rampart used in the main area — with an outer stone facing and an inner wall of timber, and in places of stone as well, enclosing a core of various earth-and-timber (chiefly chambered) construction and occurring in several variations — represents the principal Slavic fortification technique of Middle Danubian (Great Moravian) defensive architecture in the 9th century. Overall, the ramparts are estimated to have reached an average height of 1.6–2.1 m, and up to 2.1–2.6 m for the most massive reinforced earthen sections.

It is clear that the greatest effort and quantity of material were invested in the northern rampart, which cut across the almost level, easily accessible terrain of the Hornád Basin — the direction from which the site was most exposed. Together with the acropolis, which for defensive reasons necessarily formed part of a single fortified whole, the site covered roughly 5–6 hectares — comparable in size to the hillforts at Jaseňové, Devín, and Bratislava Castle.

The fortifications and material culture of the site reflect not only the regional character of the local Slavic population between the 8th and 10th centuries, but also its interactions with the Principality of Nitra and Great Moravia to the southwest, and with the Polish tribes of the Vistula region (Povislie) to the north.

Up until the mid-9th century, this was the only administrative, cultural, and economic centre in the sub-Tatra region. It then disappeared following an invasion by Great Moravian forces into Spiš. Hillfort I most likely perished in the fighting between Mojmír and Pribina — falling victim to Mojmír's efforts to subjugate Pribina's Principality of Nitra and annex it to the Moravian realm. This appears to have been a genuine war. At roughly the same time, fire destroyed the hillfort at Majcichov near Trnava, as well as more distant hillforts in the Orava region (Ostrá skala and Tupá skala — "Sharp Rock" and "Blunt Rock"). If this was all part of a single campaign — which seems very likely — then the Principality of Nitra must have been surprisingly large.

In the second half of the 9th century, new hillforts were built at Čingov (Hradisko II) and Dreveník, which endured into the 13th century. Around this time the people of Spiš adopted Christianity. Slavic culture persisted here until the region's incorporation into the Hungarian (Magyar) state.

Dating from the late 9th century and surviving into the first half of the 10th — the classic Great Moravian and post–Great Moravian period — is the second hillfort, Hillfort II (Hradisko II), at coordinates N 48°56.4423′, E 20°28.9500′. It lies about 800 m to the southwest, on the right bank of the Hornád, on a promontory tip (530–540 m above sea level) of the Čingov hill, and is known from field surveys and smaller test excavations.

Hillfort I is also passed by the yellow tourist trail no. 8737 and the green "Youth Educational Trail," which has an information panel where visitors can find the details needed to calculate the coordinates of Stage 1 [of the geocache].
